article_text:
Source: Getty Images for BFI

Mike Leigh

UK director Mike Leigh has expressed his concerns about young filmmakers in the UK not receiving the same creative freedom and control he had when he began his career.

“I’m very concerned for young filmmakers,” Leigh told Screen at the premiere of his latest film Tender Loving Care , which screened at the BFI London Film Festival on October 15.

“I’m concerned about them having the same backing and the freedom to explore and make the films they want to make in every particular detail,” he continued. “Not to be dictated to and not to be hanging round for years and years while people are bullying them about casting and the script.”

Leigh, who has been making independent films for over 50 years, said he believed the problem is only getting worse and that funders need to hand back more control to the creatives.

“Filmmakers should have the same freedom as painters and novelists and dramatists and poets and musicians to explore and create without interference,” the director stressed.

“There are plenty of people with money, but they are inhibited by relinquishing control over the material.”

Tender Loving Care won the best film award at the San Sebastian International Film Festival in September. It follows two friends who work in social care and stars Kate O’Flynn, Marion Bailey, Paul Jesson and Alice Bailey Johnson.

On whether this is to be his last film, Leigh said: “I’d love to make more films, but I have a medical condition. I’m a bit disabled, and it’s getting worse.”

The director suffers from myositis, an autoimmune disease that causes chronic muscle inflammation and weakness. He continued: “That’s all it is. It’s not a poetic or artistic affectation of some kind or a sense of doom and gloom; it’s just a fact.”

Leigh’s long-term producing partner Georgina Lowe said she hoped more audiences would watch Tender Loving Care in cinemas after a “slightly disappointing” box office for 2024’s Hard Truths , which made just shy of £900,000 in the UK and Ireland.

“I don’t think as many people went to the cinema as we would have hoped,” Lowe said. “It seems like cinema audiences are increasing again so hopefully more people will start watching indigenous films again and not just the Hollywood blockbusters.”

The BFI London Film Festival continues until October 18.

article_text:
The Busan International Film Festival drew its largest film audience in more than a decade at its 31st edition, which ran Oct. 6–15, while a political firestorm over a Korean box office hit and an Iranian director’s war speech kept politics in the spotlight.

These are Variety ’s takeaways from the festival and its Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM).

Audiences Turn Out, Market Holds Steady

Crime Thriller ‘Side Effects’ Debuts First-Look Photos and Warns About the ‘Real Killer on the Loose’: Deadly Opioids (EXCLUSIVE)

Screenings drew 200,043 admissions, the festival’s highest tally since 2015. Counting talks, outdoor events and side programs, total attendance reached 277,027, around 40,000 more than the milestone 30th edition last year. Organizers pointed to a new opening date and a bigger screening slate.

Popular on Variety

Community BIFF, the audience-programmed strand in Nampo-dong, pulled in 29,511 visitors, more than 1.7 times last year’s figure. BIFF Everywhere took films to a record 18 locations, among them Buddhist temples, traditional markets and a National Assembly building in Seoul.

The ACFM, which ran Oct. 10–13 at BEXCO under the theme “Core and Expansion,” counted 30,484 visitors, up 1.6%. Registrations climbed 4.3% to 3,158 participants from 1,266 companies in 58 countries. Exhibitors rose 17% to 339 companies, 49 of them first-timers, and Czech & Slovak and Cambodian pavilions made their debuts.

“The biggest obstacle is funding,” ACFM director Ellen Y.D. Kim told Variety . “The scale and the role of the market have grown quickly, but public support has not kept pace. National funding for ACFM has stayed at the same level for two years running.”

“For anyone who wants to work with Asia, there is no place as efficient over four days,” she said.

Korbinian Haeutle, project manager for Europe! Hub, which ran a stand with EFP and Unifrance, said the quality of the market was very good. “The meetings are good and it feels like many new distribution companies are coming up. Everyone is quite happy,” he said.

Malaysian filmmakers Woo Ming Jin, director with Greenlight Pictures, and Lau Kok Rui, director and screenwriter with Thousand Sales Pictures, said BIFF brings everybody from Asia together, “so for us it’s a very important festival.”

“You can count on everyone being here, exchanging about policy changes, sharing project updates… It’s good to see what people are doing. It’s motivational,” they said.

Politics Takes the Stage

The festival’s opening week was shadowed by “The Assassin(s),” Hur Jin-ho’s thriller about the Aug. 15, 1974 shooting of first lady Yuk Young-soo, wife of then-President Park Chung-hee. The film opened Sept. 23 and topped the Korean admissions chart, but conservative politicians and online critics accused it of distorting history.

On Oct. 1, BIFF called off “Actors House: Lee Min-ho,” a career conversation with one of the film’s stars. A day later, production company Hive Media Corp. withdrew the cast and crew from all of their festival appearances, including the opening ceremony and an outdoor stage greeting, citing the safety of audiences and attendees. The move came after a conservative group announced daily protests outside the home of lead actor Yoo Hae-jin.

The row reached the competition jury’s press conference the day after the opening ceremony, where a reporter raised the question of historical fact and creative freedom. “Specifically regarding the film you mentioned, I have not seen it, though I have noticed there are some controversies. It depends on each individual’s feelings,” jury president Zhang Yimou said. “Creation and historical truth: what does historical truth really mean? History is also written by people, so is history itself truly real? Sometimes that in itself is a question mark.”

“But as creators, we respect every creator’s vision,” he added.

Fellow juror July Jung, the director of “Next Sohee” and “Dora,” said: “What I feel now, even though it isn’t my film, is that my heart feels so cold as a filmmaker.”

Later in the festival, around 20 filmmakers, among them directors Chung Ji-young and Lee Myung-se, held a press conference in Busan urging politicians to stop using the film as a political weapon and to leave its judgment to audiences. They also criticized the main opposition People Power Party, whose 109 lawmakers had written to the Singapore International Film Festival asking it to withdraw the film. Singapore has kept “The Assassin(s)” as its Oct. 21 opening title.

Politics returned at the closing ceremony. Majidi’s “Midday Meal,” the story of a rural schoolteacher, won the Busan Award for best film from Zhang’s jury. After Zhang handed him the trophy, Majidi spoke against the war in Iran, focusing on a U.S. military strike in February on a school in Minab that killed 156 civilians, 120 of them schoolchildren. He dedicated the award to the people of Iran.

“They will stand firm to the end and fight to get their independence back,” Majidi said.

“I wish for a future with no war,” he added.

A-List Status, Star Wattage

This was Busan’s first edition since FIAPF recognized it as an A-list festival, and the second year of its competition, which featured 13 Asian titles. The win means “Midday Meal” can go straight to the Oscars’ international feature race without a national selection.

Eddie Cahyono’s Indonesian drama “Ibuku” took the special jury prize, and Lee Yun Chan won best director for Taiwan’s “To Be Ordinary.” Best actor was shared by Zhou Xun for Gu You’s “The First Taste of Loneliness” and Himeno Kashun for “Satoko Always.” Li Danfeng, sound director on “The First Taste of Loneliness,” received the artistic contribution award. Zhang’s jury also included Bi Gan, July Jung, Moon Choi, Samal Yeslyamova, Ishikawa Kei and Tran Thi Bich Ngoc.

The guest list matched the new status. Michelle Yeoh , back on the Busan red carpet after a 15-year absence, was named Asian Filmmaker of the Year at an opening ceremony hosted by Kim Minha, where Ann Hui received the Camellia Award. Former festival chair Kim Dong-ho was honored with the Korean Cinema Award. Fan Bingbing and Charlotte Gainsbourg also walked the opening night carpet, along with Alfonso Cuarón, making his first official trip to Korea.

Isabelle Huppert brought “All About Corinne,” Maggie Gyllenhaal visited Korea for the first time and Koreeda Hirokazu presented “Look Back.” Lee Chang-dong arrived with his Netflix drama “Possible Love” and its cast, Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung and Cho Yeo-jeong. Na Hong-Jin, Kim Jeewoon, Im Kwon-taek, Lee Myung-se, Bae Chang-ho, Fukada Koji, Lav Diaz, Rintaro, Reza Rahadian and Christine Hakim were also in town, as were Zhou Xun, Hyun Bin, Jung Woo-sung, Son Suk-ku, Hwang Jung-min, Kim Hye-ja and Japan’s Michieda Shunsuke.

Fan, Kim Jeewoon and cinematographer Hong Kyung-pyo curated Carte Blanche selections, while Actors’ House sessions featured Kim Go-eun, Kim Minha, Ryu Seung-ryong, Shin Min-a and Ju Ji-hoon. Gainsbourg, Gyllenhaal, Cuarón, Na, Diaz and Rintaro led master classes and talks.

Producers Close Ranks, Money Gets Creative

At Producer Hub, the Producers Guild of Korea (PGK) and Indonesian producers’ association APROFI formed the Asian Producers Alliance, with producer bodies from the Philippines, Taiwan and Hong Kong also signing on. The founders see it as the seed of a standing coalition of Asian producers working together on co-productions and policy. PGK also signed cooperation agreements with Italy’s CNA and the Sakha Filmmakers’ Union.

“Co-production used to be an option; now it is an essential strategy for sharing risk,” market chief Kim said.

New capital was on the table as well. Korean content investor Solaire Partners and Japanese entertainment financier Questry signed a memorandum of understanding on Oct. 12 to set up a Korea–Japan content fund worth KRW100 billion ($74.6 million). The market’s new Investor Summit gathered 20 companies, including Korean investor-distributors, venture capital firms and investors from Indonesia, Singapore, the U.S. and France, for a closed-door roundtable. Cinema by Brand, launched with Innocean and PGK and sponsored by Hanwha, paired three film projects with brand backing.

Financing individual films remains hard. Hollywood executives at a panel featuring UTA, Gold House, Lionsgate and HYBE saw an opening for Asian talent and stories rooted in specific cultures, while conceding that getting projects funded is still a struggle.

Kevin Law, market consultant at Film Export U.K. and a sales agent, said Busan is a steady market for keeping relationships and building partnerships. “I think one thing that’s obvious this year is that it’s difficult for independent films,” he said.

Li-yan Fan, international sales representative at France’s Ecce Films, made her first trip to Busan looking for co-production partners. “Co-production is becoming inevitable, but it still depends on the nature of each project and the resources available where you’re shooting,” Fan told Variety .

AI Gets Down to Work

Netflix has already put AI to work in some form on around 300 of its titles, Lee Sung Q, the streamer’s senior director of APAC production, said at Creative Asia, the Netflix and BIFF program for emerging talent. On the same panel, co-hosted by Netflix and the MPA, “The Outlaws” director Kang Yoon-sung put AI’s potential savings on a feature at 30% to 40% of the budget.

Kang co-directed “Run to the West,” billed as Korea’s first feature to use AI throughout production, and made a test for “The Gulf of Aden,” a film built around military operations at sea, entirely with AI using Kling. He said the savings on that film would not come only from swapping out CG. “The shoot itself got simpler, and it cut the overall production period to some extent,” he said.

He also said the technology often cuts out the debate and shared experience that filmmaking has relied on. “So the quality of the footage AI makes is very high, but when it comes to delivering emotion and moving audiences, I think we’re in a period where it has actually gotten worse,” Kang said.

Lee said that when it comes to conveying emotion, a human ultimately has to touch the work once more. “I strongly agree that a human touch is absolutely essential,” he said.

On the market floor, InnoAsia, the ACFM’s technology strand, brought in Kling, Alibaba and BytePlus. Kling teamed with filmmakers including Korean director Kim Sung-su to show how AI might reshape filmmaking, and Forum BIFF screened an AI short by Jia Zhangke. VFX veteran Hong Jae-cheol told the strand’s AI Creators Camp how images generated by AI are being slotted into production pipelines next to conventional effects, with people still steering the creative work.

“Compared to FilMart, microdramas aren’t as big as you would expect. Same for AI. In Hong Kong they were everywhere,” Haeutle said.

Law said AI remains very much a debate. “At the moment you’ll find that AI is in films but not in the way people are imagining it to be,” he said.

Europe and Thailand Build Bridges

By Europe! Hub’s count, 36% of the festival program was at least a European co-production. “There’s the 140 years France-Korean relationship and this year, the Italian Pavilion is very big,” Haeutle said.

Thailand was the ACFM’s first Country of Honor, and the Busan Story Market added five Thai titles for remake. “Compared with last year, we’ve seen many more visitors coming to our booth, asking questions and showing curiosity about what Thailand has to offer,” Phakhin Chettanat, business development manager at Thailand-based Banana Sound Studio, told Variety .

He said Asian countries are becoming more competitive, though production costs still decide where shoots go. “As talent and technical capabilities continue to improve across the region, I believe Asia will eventually become a major production hub alongside North America and Europe,” he said.

Japan was Producer Hub’s focus country this year, with Japan’s Visual Industry Promotion Organization (VIPO) co-hosting a program that drew 188 producers from 25 countries.

article_text:
Megyn Kelly was lambasted by “ The View ” hosts Whoopi Goldberg , Sara Haines and more for attacking Christina Applegate after the Emmy winner revealed she was misdiagnosed with MS. Kelly reacted to Applegate’s news on her eponymous talk show by alleging Applegate must be “crying now because I guess she no longer gets to be the face of this disease.”

“This is, like, the problem with celebrities like wanting to lean into their health problems,” Kelly said on her talk show, shading Applegate’s health journey as a “wild goose chase.”

“So, let me ask you, ma’am, you think Christina wanted to have MS so she could have a good time? Are you crazy?” Goldberg fired back on “The View,” with Haines also asking, “Who wants to be the face of MS?” (via Entertainment Weekly ).

“Talk about kicking someone when they’re down,” Haines continued. “She got a diagnosis and wanted to help other people. [She’s] now feeling the pain of not knowing what her identity is and, more importantly, what her diagnosis is. Megyn Kelly sold her soul for politics. Which one did a better job here? She literally has sunk so low in my book.”

Ana Navarro said she didn’t “even want to get into the Megyn Kelly of it all because I think she’s like a fungus that thrives on oxygen that she gets by purposely creating outrage” on sensitive topics, with Haines then calling Kelly a “bully” and Sunny Hostin slamming Kelly as “an ugly person.”

Goldberg concluded: “The idea that you would come out and say something like this, Megyn, is unbelievable, that you don’t have the wherewithal to recognize that someone is saying, ‘This is what’s happening to me. That’s how we get through our lives. We connect to each other. That’s what this is about, and I’m going to connect to you and say rethink your position on this, because you’re wrong.”

Applegate originally revealed that she had been diagnosed with MS in 2021, and retired from acting after the finale of her hit series “Dead to Me” the next year. She then become a fierce advocate for people with the disease — which causes damage to the central nervous system — and started the “MeSsy” podcast alongside “The Sopranos” star Jamie-Lynn Sigler as a way to share her experience and spread awareness.

After taking a seven-month break from the podcast, Applegate returned to the program on Oct. 21 and broke down in tears while telling listeners that new technology led to the discovery that she was misdiagnosed with MS .

“This may come as great news, but to me, I’m back at square one,” Applegate said. “It’s hard to say that [my doctor] came into my room and she said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS.’ You don’t get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I’m better. I haven’t gotten better … If anything, I’ve gotten worse in some ways. So I’m back at square one, that I don’t know what’s going on with me.”

Applegate added that “it’s weird because I feel like I let everybody down” after becoming such a big advocate for the MS community. She said that she’s still in a “state of shock,” adding: “It’s a mindfuck, for sure.”

article_text:
Non tutto ciò che può finire all’asta è destinato a essere venduto. A volte, tra le dinamiche del mercato e il valore storico di un’opera, si apre uno spazio in cui a prevalere è l’interesse per la tutela del patrimonio culturale. È quanto accade con tre dipinti giovanili di Paul Cézanne, ritirati dall’asta di Sotheby’s a Parigi in vista di un possibile ritorno ad Aix-en-Provence, la città natale dell’artista.

Le opere in questione – La Ferme, Arbres au Bord de la Rivière e Ciel Entre les Arbres – appartengono alla celebre Collezione Schlumberger e avrebbero dovuto essere vendute nell’ambito dell’asta Le Temps Retrouvé, con una stima complessiva compresa tra 1,4 e 2 milioni di euro. Un’asta da record, per una collezione leggendaria, esitata nel cuore della settimana rocambolesca di Art Basel Paris. Ma al di là del contesto: il loro ritiro è arrivato dopo le comunicazioni e le trattative, facilitate da Sotheby’s, tra la famiglia proprietaria e il Comune di Aix-en-Provence, che intende acquisirle per il Musée Granet con il sostegno del Ministero della Cultura francese.

Non si hanno ancora conferme ufficiali sul completamento dell’acquisizione. Il comunicato di Sotheby’s attesta il ritiro delle opere e l’intenzione della città di acquistarle, ma il processo è ancora in corso.

Tre dipinti, una storia da riportare a casa

Dichiarati recentemente trésors nationaux , «tesori nazionali», dal Ministero della Cultura francese, i tre Cézanne ritirati dall’asta hanno un legame profondo con Aix-en-Provence. Dipinte tra il 1862 e il 1864, facevano originariamente parte di un grande murale realizzato da Cézanne al piano terra dello Jas de Bouffan, la residenza di famiglia. L’opera era un omaggio ai grandi maestri del passato ammirati dall’artista.

Dopo la dispersione della proprietà, nel 1899, il murale fu staccato, trasferito su tela e suddiviso in otto frammenti, tra cui i tre dipinti destinati all’asta. Il loro possibile ingresso al Musée Granet consentirebbe di valorizzarli accanto ad altre opere di Cézanne, nella città che ha rappresentato per lui una casa e una fonte primaria di ispirazione.

Quando la tutela incontra il mercato

La vicenda mette al centro una questione cruciale: come conciliare il mercato dell’arte con l’interesse collettivo a conservare e rendere accessibili opere di particolare importanza storica e culturale?

Qualche mese fa, un’operazione analoga aveva interessato direttamente il patrimonio culturale italiano, quando un’opera di Antonello Da Messina era stata ritirata dall’incanto – sempre da Sotheby’s, a New York – e acquisita dallo Stato italiano per $ 14,9 milioni. Anche in questo caso francese più recente, il dialogo tra la famiglia Schlumberger, il Comune e il Ministero della Cultura – mediato dalla major Sotheby’s – ha aperto una strada alternativa.

editorial_title_zh: 「艺术雅加达2026」报告。75家画廊齐聚印尼国内外，关注与日本有关的艺术家
editorial_blocks_json:
[{"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/fe5ba2d0/IMG_2505.jpg?w=2352&q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "现场风景", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "东南亚最具代表性的艺术博览会「艺术雅加达2026（Art Jakarta 2026）」于10月2日至4日在印度尼西亚雅加达的JIExpo Kemayoran举行。今年共有来自印尼国内的42家、海外的33家共计75家画廊参加，其中19家为首次参展。东南亚地区为主，日本、韩国、台湾等亚洲各地的当代艺术作品齐聚一堂。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "继去年之后，「Korea Focus」继续推出，介绍韩国画廊，同时新增介绍印尼各地艺术社区的新板块。企业与艺术家合作的大型装置艺术等丰富多彩的项目装点了现场。本报告将关注与日本有关的艺术家作品，回顾今年的博览会。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "韩国共有14家画廊参加。连接亚洲艺术场景的博览会", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "今年，以印尼为中心，东南亚各国画廊均有参与，呈现出强化了作为国际交流场所的构成。其中值得关注的是，去年新设立的「Korea Focus」。在韩国文化体育观光部及艺术经营支援中心（KAMS）的协助下，从去年的12家画廊扩展至今年的14家，THEO、PS CENTER、GALLERY IN、Shower等均参与其中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/b0aacbc2/IMG_2575.JPG?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "现场风景", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在韩国，通过国际艺术博览会和展览，人们对现代艺术的关注度不断提高，但对画廊而言，与海外新藏家建立联系也十分重要。继续参加「Korea Focus」的PS CENTER表示，由于去年参展获得了不错的反响，因此今年也决定参加。人口众多、艺术市场有望进一步增长的印尼，已成为其拓展市场的一个重要目标。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/08e97ed8/IMG_2582.jpg?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "辛·金（Xian Kim）", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "也有与日本有联系的艺术家参与。印尼艺术家安基·普尔班多诺与阿迪·桑德罗", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本次现场，值得关注的是那些通过在日本的驻地创作和展览与日本艺术界建立联系的印尼艺术家的作品。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "其中一位是驻扎在日惹的安基·普尔班多诺（Angki Purbandono）。安基以使用扫描仪而非相机创作图像的「扫描摄影」技法而闻名。他扫描日常物品和自然物，创造出新的图像。2009年他曾参加「第四届福冈亚洲艺术三年展」，与日本的交流历史悠久。今年的艺术雅加达上，他通过SAL Project发表了大型装置作品《Berbunga-bunga: Tribute to Red Cross Movement in South Papua》（2026）。
", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作品结合了扫描摄影图像、灯箱和竹子。灵感来源于南巴布亚原住民保护土地和森林的运动，作品以土地权利和环境问题为背景，通过鲜艳的花朵图像，展现了印尼所面临的社问题。

article_text:
東南アジアを代表するアートフェア「アート・ジャカルタ2026（Art Jakarta 2026）」が、10月2日から4日まで、インドネシア・ジャカルタのJIExpo Kemayoranで開催された。今年はインドネシア国内から42、海外から33の計75ギャラリーが参加し、そのうち19ギャラリーが初出展。東南アジアを中心に、日本、韓国、台湾などアジア各地の現代アートが一堂に会した。

昨年に続き、韓国のギャラリーを紹介する「Korea Focus」が展開されたほか、インドネシア各地のアートコミュニティを紹介する新セクションも登場。企業とアーティストによる大型インスタレーションなど、多彩なプログラムが会場を彩った。本レポートでは、日本とゆかりのあるアーティストの作品にも注目しながら、今年のフェアを振り返る。

韓国から14ギャラリーが参加。アジアのアートシーンをつなぐフェア

今年もインドネシアを中心に、東南アジア各国のギャラリーが参加。国際的な交流の場としての役割を強く感じさせる構成となった。なかでも注目したいのが、昨年新設された「Korea Focus」だ。韓国文化体育観光部および芸術経営支援センター（KAMS）の協力によって展開され、昨年の12ギャラリーから今年は14ギャラリーへと規模を拡大し、THEO、PS CENTER、GALLERY IN、Showerなどが参加した。

韓国では国際的なアートフェアや展覧会を通じて現代アートへの注目が高まっているが、ギャラリーにとっては海外の新たなコレクターとの接点をつくることも重要だ。昨年に引き続き「Korea Focus」に参加したPS CENTERに話を聞くと、昨年の出展で手応えを感じたことから、今年も参加を決めたという。人口規模が大きく、アート市場のさらなる成長が期待されるインドネシアは、その進出先のひとつとなっている。

日本とのつながりがある作家も参加。インドネシアのアーティスト、アンキ・プルバンドノとアディ・スンドロ

今回の会場では、日本での滞在制作や展覧会などを通じて、日本のアートシーンとつながりを持つインドネシア人アーティストの作品にも注目したい。

そのひとりが、ジョグジャカルタを拠点に活動するアンキ・プルバンドノ（Angki Purbandono）だ。アンキは、カメラの代わりにスキャナーを用いてイメージを制作する「スキャノグラフィー」という手法で知られるアーティスト。身近な物や自然物をスキャンし、新たなイメージを生み出してきた。2009年には「第4回福岡アジア美術トリエンナーレ」に参加するなど、日本との交流も長い。今年のアート・ジャカルタでは、SAL Projectから大型インスタレーション《Berbunga-bunga: Tribute to Red Cross Movement in South Papua》（2026）を発表した。

作品は、スキャノグラフィーによるイメージとライトボックス、竹を組み合わせたもの。南パプアの先住民による土地や森林を守る運動に着想を得ており、土地の権利や環境問題を背景に持つ。鮮やかな花々のイメージとともに、インドネシアが抱える社会的な問題を提示する作品となっている。

もうひとりが、SEWU SATUのブースで個展形式で紹介されていたアディ・スンドロ（Adi Sundoro）だ。1992年ジャカルタ生まれのアディは、版画を中心に、印刷という技法を拡張しながら制作を続けている。日常生活のなかにある些細な出来事や社会制度に着目し、印刷物や身近な素材を通じて、社会の仕組みを考察する作品を発表してきた。

アディは2025年には 国際芸術センター青森（ACAC） のアーティスト・イン・レジデンス・プログラムに参加。インドネシアで日常的に食べられる揚げ物「ゴレンガン」の包装紙に、個人情報を含む書類が再利用されていることに着目し、日本とインドネシアにおける情報管理やプライバシーに対する意識の違いを探究した。また、同年にはジャカルタの美術館、Museum MACANの子供向けアートスペースのプロジェクトにも参加するなど、活動の幅を広げている。

インドネシアのアーティストが日本での滞在制作を通して新たな視点を獲得し、その経験を作品へとつなげていく。こうした交流も、アジアの現代アートシーンを支える重要な要素のひとつだ。

企業とアーティストのコラボレーションを積極的に

アート・ジャカルタの特徴のひとつが、企業とアーティストによる積極的なコラボレーションだ。フェアの主要パートナーには、スイスのプライベート銀行ジュリアス・ベア（Julius Baer）や、インドネシアの金融機関BCA、投資サービスを展開するBibitとStockbitなどが名を連ねる。企業はたんにフェアを資金面で支援するだけでなく、アーティストと協働し、作品やインスタレーションを発表している。

デジタル金投資プラットフォーム大手のTreasuryは、エッツァ・メイシャラ（Etza Meisyara）と協働し、《Gravity of the Unheld》を発表。金が持つ物質的な価値に加え、人々がそこに見出す意味や精神性を、複数の感覚に働きかけるインスタレーションを通じて表現した。

そのほか、MINIとファッションブランドPaul Smithの取り組みなど、金融からファッション、ライフスタイルまで、幅広い企業がアートフェアに参加している。今年も企業がアーティストの創造性を取り入れながら、来場者に新しい体験を提供する姿勢が印象的だった。企業が現代アートに関わることは、アーティストの制作を支えるだけでなく、普段はアートに触れる機会の少ない人々との接点を生み出すことにもつながっている。

アート・ジャカルタが特徴的なのは、インドネシアのアートシーンを基盤としながら、海外との交流や地域のコミュニティ、企業とのコラボレーションを積極的に取り入れている点だ。作品を売買する場であることはもちろん、異なる国や地域のアーティスト、ギャラリー、コレクターが出会い、新たな関係を築いていく。アジアの現代アートが多様な広がりを見せるいま、アート・ジャカルタは東南アジアのアートシーンをつなぐ重要なプラットフォームとして、その存在感を高めている。

article_text:
Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography, a new exhibition at Tate Modern, showcases the history of pictorialism and how it expanded the possibilities of photography as an art form

A serene landscape showing splashing white ducks who seem to merge seamlessly with the babbling water, shadowy trees looming like dark mountains. This photograph, part of Tate Modern’s exhibition Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography , was taken by Liu Bannong in 1927 after the Chinese photographer returned from studying linguistics in Paris, where pictorialism was pursued by artists running their own salons, and publishing magazines on art photography. Pictorialism was the first move towards proclaiming photography an art form yet, until now, its impact on image-making practice in south-east and south Asia has been relatively unknown. The Tate’s exhibition fills these lacunae by looking at this movement as transcontinental.

Pictorialism was initially theorised by English photographer Henry Peach Robinson, whose 1869 instructional book Pictorial Effect in Photography urged image-makers to follow the order and composition in painting, rather than simply documenting reality. Armed with such influences Bannong produced a text of his own – Bannong tanying (‘ Bannong’s Comments on Photography’ ) – which drew from the aesthetic discourse of traditional Chinese painting. It argued for photography as an expressive medium revealing an inner world of emotion. This dialogue was continued by others, including Long Chin-San, whose essay Photography and Chinese Painting (1955) advised ‘choosing’ the good parts of a photograph, emulating the approach of traditional Chinese art.

“Contemporary photographic art is where it is today due to the efforts by pictorialists to carve out a space for photography within fine art” – Charmaine Toh, curator

The ‘selection’ Chin-San referred to is seen in Singaporean Lee Sow Lim’s early work, which uses layers of photo negatives to arrive at a single image. Transferring an ethereal quality from Chinese ink paintings into photographic imagery, Sow Lim even stamped the results with a traditional painterly red seal. His later works are abstractions in colour – Singaporean artist Tan Lip Seng’s works were figurative but, created with layers of high contrast and highly saturated colour transparencies, were equally innovative. Not all pictorialists were in favour of manipulated images. British writer and photographer PH Emerson favoured naturalism, controlling light and composition to create beauty – as did Singaporean Yip Cheong Fun, in his portraits of fishermen and children.

None of this was happening in isolation, but within photo clubs and salons in south-east and south Asia with an interest in pictorialism that continued long after modernist photography had taken over in the West. Many camera clubs had initially started as forums for colonial officials and local amateur photographers, building information for British administrators; Photographic Societies of Bombay (1854) and Bengal (1856) conducted ethnographic studies, for example. But, points out Charmaine Toh, senior curator of international art (photography) at the Tate and curator of the Tate Modern show, “these clubs started at a time when most of south-east Asia was on the verge of independence”, and pictorialism for many offered a deviation from the surveying gaze. It also allowed the opportunity to showcase worldwide as these salons had access to journals with details for open calls.

While pictorialism changed the language of ethnographic photography in Elli Sougioultzoglou-Seraidari’s images of refugees in Attica in the mid-1920s, it also allowed photographers in the colonies alternative approaches to self-representation. They set up other societies, such as the Photographic Society of India (1937), co-founded by mill-worker Dhirajlal R Mody, or the Photographic Society of Ceylon (1935) by Sri Lankan photographer Lionel Wendt. Wendt’s portraits of the male body in the 1930s and early 1940s introduced fluidity and homoeroticism, depicting men far beyond their castes and professions. The images departed from the buttoned-up ethnographic representations – though Toh warns against drawing easy conclusions, pointing out that the body was still performing in Wendt’s work, re-rehearsing privileged stereotypes.

“Some photographers would continue using colonial ‘tropes’, like photographing someone in a sarong in Malaysia, to get accepted into exhibitions overseas,” explains Toh. “It was a certain agency as they played up to Western expectations and then won awards at international salons. This was important to see themselves as entering a new era of postcolonial modernity.” Wendt sent his works to London or Paris, the colonial centres at the time; even so, his works and images by others have not been included in the history of pictorialism.

“Piecing together this history is on-ground work and opening boxes,” says Toh, whose research included meeting with photographers’ families to find long-lost archives and prints. “The RPS Collection became a major resource as these photographers would send their prints to London for the RPS annual exhibition – and didn’t ask for them back,” she adds. “Behind these prints is an entire history of where it has travelled to, even between countries who weren’t getting along diplomatically.”

And, while pictorialism arguably never went away, contemporary preoccupations with the ideology of a certain photographic gaze, or with questioning the medium more generally, owe much to these predecessors. “Contemporary photographic art is where it is today due to the efforts by pictorialists to carve out a space for photography within fine art,” reflects Toh.

Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography is at Tate Modern , London, until 21 February 2027.

照片公司孟买(1854年)和孟加拉(1856年)进行的民族学研究,例如。“这些俱乐部在东南亚大部分处于独立边缘时开始了”,许多人对图像主义提出了从调查中脱离的偏见,这也允许在全球范围内展出,因为这些展览会有访问开放通话的详细信息的杂志。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/ID_003_Liu-Bannong-The-Suburb-1927.-Private-Collection.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "原名:The Suburb, 1927 © Liu Bannong.", "credit": "British Journal of Photography", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在1920年代中期,图像主义改变了以色列摄影的语言,而在1920年代中期埃利·苏吉奥·佐格卢·塞拉达里(Elli Sougioultzoglou-Seraidari)的图像中,它也允许殖民地的摄影师采取替代自我代表性的方法,他们建立了其他社会,如印度摄影协会(Indian Photographic Society,1937年),由千工人Dhirajlal R Mody共同创立,或斯里兰摄影师Lionel Wendt(Sri Lankan Photographic Society,1935年)的塞隆摄影协会。1930年代和1940年代初的男性身体的肖像引入了流动性和同性恋,描绘了男人远远超越他们的作品和职业。 这些图像从按钮上传的种族形象中脱颖而出 - 尽管托赫警告不做出轻松的结论,指出身体仍然在温特特的工作中表现出来,重新听到特权的类型。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“一些摄影师将继续使用殖民地的“天花板”,如在马来西亚的萨龙里拍摄某人,以接受海外展览,”Toh解释道,“这是一个特定的机构,因为他们符合西方的期望,然后赢得了国际展览会的奖项,这很重要,认为自己进入一个新的殖民后现代时代。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“把这个故事聚集在一起是地面工作和打开盒子,”Toh说,他的研究包括与摄影师的家人会面,寻找长期丢失的档案和印刷。 “RPS收藏成为一个重要的资源,因为这些摄影师将他们的印刷到伦敦为RPS年度展览 - 并没有要求他们回来,”她补充道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "虽然画家主义可能从未消失,但当代对某种摄影气体的意识形态或对媒体更普遍的质疑的担忧,对这些先驱有很大的债务,“当代摄影艺术是因为画家们在美术中为摄影创造一个空间而努力,而现在是因为它在美术中创造了一个空间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "光与魔法:艺术摄影的诞生在伦敦泰特现代,直到2027年2月21日。", "links": [{"text": "Tate Modern", "url": "https://www.tate.org.uk/"}], "translated": true}]

article_text:
The SAG-AFTRA board voted Saturday to extend the contract of Duncan Crabtree-Ireland , the union’s national executive director, for four years and to add CEO to his title.

Crabtree-Ireland’s contract was set to expire in 2028, but will now run through June 20, 2032. The financial terms of the agreement were not disclosed. He was paid $1.1 million for the 2026 fiscal year.

The extension will carry Crabtree-Ireland through the next round of negotiations with the major studios, with the current deal set to expire in June 2030. In a statement, the union said that the extension will offer “added stability and continuity for the union during a time of unprecedented industry disruption.”

Crabtree-Ireland has spent nearly his entire career at SAG-AFTRA, serving as general counsel and chief operating officer before being named national executive director in 2021. He has made artificial intelligence a key focus of the union’s negotiations, reaching a series of agreements that aim to allow performers to capture the upside of AI while protecting them from unauthorized uses of their likenesses. He was also a central figure in the 2023 actors’ strike.

Popular on Variety

Sean Astin, the president of SAG-AFTRA, praised Crabtree-Ireland in a statement after the vote.

“To battle giant global transnational corporations, we need expert leadership with a track record of successful bargaining and significant operational management expertise,” Astin said. “That is Duncan. He is a powerful executive who has led our union at the bargaining table, in the halls of Congress and in boardrooms and conference rooms across the industry and the world. We are thrilled to have guaranteed Duncan’s continued service to the members of SAG-AFTRA.”

The extension was approved with 98.34% of the board in favor in a weighted vote.

“Leading SAG-AFTRA’s staff is the honor of my career, and I’m grateful for the opportunity to keep doing this work,” Crabtree-Ireland said. “As we continue fighting for human creativity, the coming years will be crucial for charting the path forward. I intend to fight alongside our leadership to make sure our members control their image, likeness, voice, and destiny in the workplace, and that they are compensated fairly in the process. I thank President Astin, the national officers, and the National Board for their trust, and our extraordinary staff team for everything they make possible.”

Pictured: Duncan Crabtree-Ireland (left) and SAG-AFTRA President Sean Astin.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 桑莱·索里的彩色摄影作品首次在伦敦展出，展现了一位杰出的肖像摄影师，他长期生活在塞杜·凯塔和马利克·西迪贝的阴影之下。L’article Sanlé Sory, the Faces of Burkina in Color est apparu en premier sur Blind Magazine .
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "桑莱·索里（Sanlé Sory）从他拍摄第一张证件照的那天起，便与摄影结下了不解之缘。1960年，经过数年的学徒生涯，这位17岁的年轻人在此国第二大城市博博迪乌拉索（Bobo-Dioulasso）开设了自己的照相馆——沃尔塔照相馆（Volta Photo）。同年，作为西非前法国殖民地的上沃尔塔（Upper Volta）赢得了独立；其革命总统托马斯·桑卡拉（Thomas Sankara）于1984年将其更名为布基纳法索（Burkina Faso）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这家照相馆再简陋不过了：一块用作背景的布料、一张脚下反复出现的花纹地毯、一辆在各个肖像照中不断重现的摩托车。偶尔会有一幅手绘布景滑入镜头，那是一个错视画法（trompe l’oeil）的立面，正如策展人陶斯·达马尼（Taous Dahmani）所说，它提供了“充满旅行、野心与可能性的想象世界”。不过，更多的色彩来自拍摄对象本身，他们从发型到姿态都精心构图。桑莱·索里也并不局限于照相馆内；他还会在墙外拍摄他的拍摄对象，穿梭于货摊的织物或卖鞋者的货架之间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "伦敦的展览将一切押注在色彩上——这位摄影师此前一直以黑白作品闻名，他在1980年代中期转向了彩色。他用一句俏皮话总结了自己的这种转变：“当你身处一个每个人都在跳舞的地方时，你也必须试着像其他人一样跳舞！”色彩契合了一个处于全面狂热中的社会，在那里，时尚、音乐和态度定下了基调。在他那高饱和度的胶片上，织物熠熠生辉，太阳镜闪闪发光。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "历史可以从人们的穿着中读懂。两名女性摆出姿势，她们穿着2010年为纪念独立50周年而印有“Burkina Faso, 50 ans”字样的蜡染印花连衣裙。一名青少年穿着印有贝拉克·奥巴马（Barack Obama）肖像的T恤，奥巴马于2008年当选为美国首位黑人总统，这个偶像的影响力远至博博迪乌拉索的街头。在其他地方，一件摩纳哥AS球衣或一件布基纳法索足球衫彰显了球迷的忠诚。正如这位摄影师喜欢回忆的那样，在他的照相馆里，“宗教人士、艺术家、音乐家以及每一个人都可以成为英雄。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/sanle-sory-volta-photo-studio-bobo-dioulasso-burkina-faso-sanle-sory-2026.-courtesy-of-tezeta-4-683x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Volta Photo Studio, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso © Sanlé Sory, 2026. article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sanlé Sory came to photography the day he sat for an identity photograph. In 1960, after several years as an apprentice, the seventeen-year-old opened his own studio, Volta Photo, in Bobo-Dioulasso, the country’s second city. That same year, Upper Volta, a former French colony in West Africa, gained its independence; its revolutionary president, Thomas Sankara, would rename it Burkina Faso in 1984."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The studio could not be plainer: a length of cloth for a backdrop, a patterned mat that recurs underfoot, a motorcycle that returns from one portrait to the next. Now and then a painted scene slips in, a trompe l’oeil façade offering what curator Taous Dahmani calls “imagined worlds of travel, ambition and possibility.” More often, though, the color comes from the sitters themselves, who compose their image with care, from hairstyle to pose. Nor does Sanlé Sory keep to the studio; he also photographs his subjects beyond its walls, among the fabrics of a stall or the shelves of a shoe seller."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The London show stakes everything on color, a turn the photographer, until then known for his work in black and white, made in the mid-1980s. He sums up his conversion with a quip: “When you are in a place where everybody dances, you have to try to dance like everyone else!” Color weds a society in full ferment, where fashion, music and attitude set the tone. On his saturated film, fabrics blaze and sunglasses gleam."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "History can be read in what people wear. Two women pose in dresses cut from the wax print marking fifty years of independence, in 2010, stamped “Burkina Faso, 50 ans.” A teenager sports a T-shirt bearing the likeness of Barack Obama, elected in 2008 as the first Black president of the United States, an icon as far away as the streets of Bobo-Dioulasso. Elsewhere, an AS Monaco jersey or a Burkinabè football shirt proclaims a fan’s allegiance. In his studio, the photographer likes to recall, “religious people, artists, musicians, and everyone could become a hero.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/sanle-sory-volta-photo-studio-bobo-dioulasso-burkina-faso-sanle-sory-2026.-courtesy-of-tezeta-4-683x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Volta Photo Studio, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Two men there brought the African studio into the history of art. Seydou Keïta (1921–2001) photographed Bamako’s rising middle class from the 1950s on, in black and white, leaning against an automobile or a radio set, draped in their finest boubous. Malick Sidibé (1935–2016), “the eye of Bamako,” caught the youth of the independence-era parties, all twist and bell-bottoms, before receiving, in 2007, the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Biennale, the first photographer to be so honored. The West had crowned them fathers of the studio portrait as early as the 1990s."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sanlé Sory belongs to the same lineage, but he long remained its forgotten link: a provincial photographer, a convert to color, passed over by the official record. One idea animates him nonetheless, and his peers alike. The Cameroonian Samuel Fosso (born 1962) casts himself as a dandy, a liberated woman or a hero of the Black cause. The Senegalese Omar Victor Diop (born 1980) restages, in sumptuous self-portraits, the African figures erased from the schoolbooks. The Moroccan Hassan Hajjaj (born 1961), finally, turns the studio into a pop carnival, where fabrics from the souk rub shoulders with subverted luxury logos. With them as with him, before the lens, anyone at all can become the king of his own image."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Unlike theirs, though, Sanlé Sory’s work nearly vanished. On the trail of Burkina Faso’s forgotten music, the French writer and record collector Florent Mazzoleni eventually found the photographer, whose portraits had graced the album covers of Volta Jazz, the city’s foremost band. He came upon him burning his old negatives, mere castoffs in his eyes. Mazzoleni rescued crates of them, then spent years sifting through an archive of some 200,000 negatives."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Recognition followed. In 2018, the Art Institute of Chicago gave him his first solo exhibition in an American museum. Now, in 2026, two books appear, Volta Colour (GOST), devoted to these color years, and a monograph from Phaidon, just as The Photographers’ Gallery brings together his prints, record sleeves and all. article_text:
Sanlé Sory came to photography the day he sat for an identity photograph. In 1960, after several years as an apprentice, the seventeen-year-old opened his own studio, Volta Photo, in Bobo-Dioulasso, the country’s second city. That same year, Upper Volta, a former French colony in West Africa, gained its independence; its revolutionary president, Thomas Sankara, would rename it Burkina Faso in 1984.

The studio could not be plainer: a length of cloth for a backdrop, a patterned mat that recurs underfoot, a motorcycle that returns from one portrait to the next. Now and then a painted scene slips in, a trompe l’oeil façade offering what curator Taous Dahmani calls “imagined worlds of travel, ambition and possibility.” More often, though, the color comes from the sitters themselves, who compose their image with care, from hairstyle to pose. Nor does Sanlé Sory keep to the studio; he also photographs his subjects beyond its walls, among the fabrics of a stall or the shelves of a shoe seller.

The London show stakes everything on color, a turn the photographer, until then known for his work in black and white, made in the mid-1980s. He sums up his conversion with a quip: “When you are in a place where everybody dances, you have to try to dance like everyone else!” Color weds a society in full ferment, where fashion, music and attitude set the tone. On his saturated film, fabrics blaze and sunglasses gleam.

History can be read in what people wear. Two women pose in dresses cut from the wax print marking fifty years of independence, in 2010, stamped “Burkina Faso, 50 ans.” A teenager sports a T-shirt bearing the likeness of Barack Obama, elected in 2008 as the first Black president of the United States, an icon as far away as the streets of Bobo-Dioulasso. Elsewhere, an AS Monaco jersey or a Burkinabè football shirt proclaims a fan’s allegiance. In his studio, the photographer likes to recall, “religious people, artists, musicians, and everyone could become a hero.”

To take the measure of his singularity, a detour through neighboring Mali is in order. Two men there brought the African studio into the history of art. Seydou Keïta (1921–2001) photographed Bamako’s rising middle class from the 1950s on, in black and white, leaning against an automobile or a radio set, draped in their finest boubous. Malick Sidibé (1935–2016), “the eye of Bamako,” caught the youth of the independence-era parties, all twist and bell-bottoms, before receiving, in 2007, the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Biennale, the first photographer to be so honored. The West had crowned them fathers of the studio portrait as early as the 1990s.

Sanlé Sory belongs to the same lineage, but he long remained its forgotten link: a provincial photographer, a convert to color, passed over by the official record. One idea animates him nonetheless, and his peers alike. The Cameroonian Samuel Fosso (born 1962) casts himself as a dandy, a liberated woman or a hero of the Black cause. The Senegalese Omar Victor Diop (born 1980) restages, in sumptuous self-portraits, the African figures erased from the schoolbooks. The Moroccan Hassan Hajjaj (born 1961), finally, turns the studio into a pop carnival, where fabrics from the souk rub shoulders with subverted luxury logos. With them as with him, before the lens, anyone at all can become the king of his own image.

Unlike theirs, though, Sanlé Sory’s work nearly vanished. On the trail of Burkina Faso’s forgotten music, the French writer and record collector Florent Mazzoleni eventually found the photographer, whose portraits had graced the album covers of Volta Jazz, the city’s foremost band. He came upon him burning his old negatives, mere castoffs in his eyes. Mazzoleni rescued crates of them, then spent years sifting through an archive of some 200,000 negatives.

Recognition followed. In 2018, the Art Institute of Chicago gave him his first solo exhibition in an American museum. Now, in 2026, two books appear, Volta Colour (GOST), devoted to these color years, and a monograph from Phaidon, just as The Photographers’ Gallery brings together his prints, record sleeves and all. Past eighty, Sanlé Sory steps at last into his full light.

“Sanlé Sory: Colour Years” is at The Photographers’ Gallery in London from October 14, 2026 to February 21, 2027. Two new books Sanlé Sory (Phaidon) and Volta Colour (GOST) will also be available in October 2026.

article_text:
Strength in numbers? Movie theater operators are hoping the adage proves true as four new movies aim to bolster the October box office.

Paramount’s video game adaptation “ Street Fighter ” will lead over fellow newcomers, with opening weekend estimates of $25 million to $35 million from 3,500 North American theaters. Disney’s survival thriller “ Whalefall ” should secure second place with $10 million to $12 million from 3,065 venues. Meanwhile A24’s much-hyped Elizabeth Holmes documentary “ You Can See Everything ” is aiming for a strong $7 million to $8 million from just 800 locations, and the Focus Features remake of Jane Austen’s “Sense and Sensibility” is targeting $5 million to $8 million from 2,436 screens.

Related Stories

Although “Street Fighter” is projected to claim the No. 1 spot, the PG-13 action-adventure carries the biggest budget among the quartet and will need to stick around in theaters to justify its price tag. Legendary and video game developer Capcom co-financed the film for $82 million, with Paramount only on the hook for distribution. The long-gestating “Street Fighter” was originally set at Sony as part of Legendary’s pact with the studio and moved to Paramount once the initial deal expired. Overseas, “Street Fighter” is projected to earn roughly $35 million from 65 markets.

“Street Fighter” is the third movie based on the Capcom video game series. The first live-action film, released in 1994 and starred Jean-Claude Van Damme, was box office hit with $100 million, not adjusted for inflation. The second, 2009’s “Street Fighter: The Legend of Chun-Li,” was a major misfire for 20th Century, earning just $12.8 million against a $50 million budget. This reboot, directed by Kitao Sakurai and starring Noah Centineo and Andrew Koji, takes place in 1993 as two estranged fighters are recruited to enter a tournament that forces them to face off against each other.

“Whalefall” cost $60 million and also requires substantial staying power, since theater owners keep about half of ticket sales. Directed by Brian Duffield, “Whalefall” follows a scuba diver (Austin Abrams) who is swallowed by a sperm whale and has only one hour of oxygen left in his tank as he figures out how to escape. Reviews have been mostly positive, with one critic calling the film “ amusing genre pulp .”

“You Can See Everything” cost around $7 million to produce, and exhibitors believe the movie could become the rare breakout documentary. Earlier this year, Amazon MGM’s “Melania,” a $40-million-budgeted glimpse at first lady Melania Trump, landed the biggest opening for a non-music or concert doc in over a decade with $7.1 million from 1,778 theaters. Most non-fiction films, however, would be lucky these days to earn that much by the end of their box office runs.

Hype for “You Can See Everything” has been high since A24 unveiled the top-secret project at Telluride Film Festival in early September. Comedian Nathan Fielder and “Primetime” filmmaker Lance Oppenheim quietly worked for more than three years on the movie, which offers an unhinged look at the Theranos founder a month before she began an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors. The doc will benefit from stellar reviews and positive word-of-mouth; it holds a 100% on Rotten Tomatoes, with Variety’s Owen Gleiberman describing the unconventional story as a “one-of-a-kind [ …] circus.”

“Sense and Sensibility,” which carries a $25 million budget, hopes to serve as counterprogramming against the male-skewing “Street Fighter” and “Whalefall.” Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles star in the latest adaptation of the Jane Austen classic as sisters Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, who navigate love, loss and financial uncertainty as they are forced to leave their family estate in Sussex.

“Sense and Sensibility” has been reworked for the screen a number of times, most notably with director Ang Lee’s 1995 film starring Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet as Elinor and Marianne Dashwood. That film was a critical and commercial smash, earning seven Oscar nominations and generating $135 million at the box office, not adjusted for inflation. Focus Features over the years has backed two prior remakes of Austen’s work, including the 2005 version of “Pride and Prejudice” with Keira Knightley and Matthew Macfadyen as well as 2020’s “Emma,” which starred Anya-Taylor Joy. The well-reviewed “Emma” was released digitally while theaters were closed due to the pandemic.

So far, the October box office has been uneven. Tom Cruise’s dark comedy “Digger” and Aaron Sorkin’s Facebook drama “The Social Reckoning” flopped, while Colleen Hoover adaptation “Verity” and “Other Mommy” with Jessica Chastain are shaping up to be modest wins. Luckily, it won’t take much to improve upon last October, which hit a three-decade low amid a pileup of disasters including Dwayne Johnson’s MMA drama “The Smashing Machine” and Disney’s sci-fi sequel “Tron: Ares.”

article_text:
Filme terá direção de Paul King, de "As Aventuras de Paddington".

A próxima grande cinebiografia de Hollywood está tomando forma. Sabrina Carpenter e Margaret Qualley se juntaram a Tom Holland no elenco do filme sobre a vida de Fred Astaire (via Deadline ).

Qualley interpretará Adele Astaire, irmã de Fred, e Carpenter interpretará Ginger Rogers. Fred e Adele foram grandes estrelas da Broadway e do West End em Londres antes de Fred Astaire se tornar uma das maiores estrelas do cinema ao lado de sua parceira de dança, Rogers. O desdobramento ocorre quase cinco anos depois de Holland revelar, pela primeira vez, que lideraria o projeto.

Paul King, de “As Aventuras de Paddington”, dirige o filme e assina o roteiro junto a Steven Levenson, baseando-se no livro “The Astaires: Fred & Adele”, de Kathleen Riley. Riley também atua como consultora de roteiro e história no filme, que tem ainda o apoio de Ava Astaire McKenzie, filha de Fred; seu filho, Tyler McKenzie, é consultor e coprodutor do filme.

Ainda não há previsão de estreia para a cinebiografia de Fred Astaire.
